episodes.213898: A plume of monsoon moisture between an upper low over the Permian Basin of western Texas and southeast New Mexico and a disturbance over Arizona resulted in diurnal shower and thunderstorm activity first across the higher terrain before moving south and west into nearby highlands and valley locations. Thunderstorms producing locally heavy rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches resulted in flash flooding in Gallup and Zuni Pueblo during the evening hours of July 16th. Heavy rainfall amounts of up to 2 inches on the South Fork burn scar just west of Ruidoso on July 17th resulted in flash flooding and debris flows on and downstream of the Cedar Creek area. A low water crossing flooded from heavy rains in northwestern Roswell on the 18th, while storms producing flash flooding impacted areas just northeast of Grants, NM on the 19th.
episodes.213971: On the afternoon of July 17, a thunderstorm moved southward from Walker County into Jefferson County, producing a few instances of minor tree damage around Empire and Bagley. Also associated with this thunderstorm, numerous photos and videos were taken of a funnel-like cloud. One video showed what appeared to be a very brief and small condensation funnel in an open field behind homes on Daniel Trail. This funnel produced no damage and was determined to be a brief gustnado occurring under the shelf cloud of the larger thunderstorm.||More afternoon thunderstorms on July 18 and 19 produced minor tree damage across a few counties.
episodes.214062: Isolated thunderstorm developed over Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening of July 16, 2026. The combination of very heavy rainfall and slow-moving or stationary thunderstorms resulted in flooding across portions of Overton County.
episodes.214066: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening of July 17, 2026. The combination of heavy rain and slow-moving and training thunderstorms caused flooding across portions of Middle Tennessee. The most significant flooding was reported in Cookeville where 3 to 4 inches of rain caused flash flooding on several roadways.
episodes.214205: A stalled stationary boundary sparked showers and thunderstorms across the Ohio Valley region before eventually lifting north as a warm front. A very moist airmass was in place and storms produced heavy rainfall, leading to flooding.
episodes.214223: The overall synoptic pattern featured the subtropical high over the Central Rockies with easterly flow over most of the region. On the southern periphery of the subtropical high, an easterly wave traversed the region helping to increase the forcing for ascent and thus the potential for more widespread convective activity. A very moist airmass was present as PWAT values ranged between 1.8-2.2 across most of the lower elevations of central and southern AZ. The very moist airmass combined with MLCAPE values of around 500 J/KG was sufficient for the development of thunderstorms to produce heavy rainfall rates in excess of 1-2 per hour. With the flow aloft being on the weak side, with the steering motion at most 5 kts, the thunderstorm activity that developed was very slow moving, exacerbating the flood threat. During the evening hours on the 16th and continuing through the early morning hours on the 17th, a complex of thunderstorms developed just east of Phoenix, affecting much of the foothills and higher terrain areas before activity gradually clustered to the north of Phoenix metro and gradually weakening during the morning hours on the 17th. Another area of thunderstorms with heavy rainfall developed during the late morning/early afternoon hours across portions of southern Gila County, mainly between the Globe and San Carlos area. When all set and done, widespread amounts of 1-3 were observed with some areas along SR-88 between Tortilla Flat and Roosevelt Lake observing in excess of 4 based on rain gauge observations and doppler radar estimates, with much of the rainfall occurring within 1-3 hours. The heavy rainfall in this short time span lead to several flash flood incidents. In addition, during the afternoon hours on the 17th, an isolated nearly stationary severe storm developed east of Parker, AZ producing multiple inches of rain, causing the Bill Williams River to rise very rapidly and come within 0.50 feet of the gauge's historical peak, as well as a very large tree to be uprooted near the River Lodge Resort located south of the Parker Strip along the Lower Colorado River Valley.
episodes.214402: Monsoon storms formed during the afternoon bringing heavy rains and some flash flooding.
episodes.214403: Heavy rain from monsoon storms brought multiple rounds of flash flooding including in many populated areas.
episodes.214774: The synoptic pattern shifted by mid July sufficiently to allow a more marked influx of monsoonal moisture into Utah. In addition to some isolated thunderstorm wind gusts, this resulted in numerous instances of flash flooding and debris flows.
episodes.214846: Typical summer weather prevailed with scattered afternoon and evening storms, some of which were severe.
episodes.214952: Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced several wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.215259: A deep, tight closed low pressure system over the Olympics interacted with a very wet monsoon ridge. The region experienced unusually high precipitable water, and dew points in the fifties indicated that moisture was present through a deep layer of the atmosphere.
episodes.215262: An upper low near the Olympics continued to pump moist and unstable air across the Northern Rockies leading to scattered to widespread thunderstorms.
episodes.215531: Repeated rounds of thunderstorms resulted in rainfall of 2 to 4 inches in portions of Marshall and Miami counties. A flood advisory was issued and instances of road closures were noted.
episodes.215718: A strong upper-level ridge moved over the northern Great Plains allowing a moist, tropical airmass to move over South-Central Texas. Precipitable water values increased to greater than 2.0 inches which were near or above the 95th percentile of climatological values for this part of July. Multiple rounds of excessive rainfall were triggered by mid-level disturbances around the southern periphery of the high and low-level outflow boundaries. This convection was aided by nocturnal low-level jet streaks which led to slow moving, back building thunderstorms. Most of South-Central Texas received more than two inches of rain. The greatest totals were over Uvalde and Kinney Counties where 20-30 inches occurred. Another local maximum of 15-20 inches was observed in central Kerr County. Ten to 15 inches were widespread from Del Rio to Hondo and northward to northeastern Edwards to western Gillespie Counties. Damage estimates were near $115 million across South-Central Texas.
episodes.215850: A few storms developed ahead of a cold front across northeastern Minnesota during the afternoon of the 17th. The strongest storms moved across southern St. Louis County into the Gary-New Duluth area and produced damaging wind gusts in spots that resulted in downed trees and power poles.
episodes.215851: A few storms developed ahead of a cold front across northeastern Minnesota during the afternoon of the 17th and moved into northwestern Wisconsin. These storms produced damaging wind gusts as they moved eastward, with one storm crossing the Bayfield Peninsula and then through Ashland producing damage to buildings on the east side of town along the lakefront.
episodes.215942: A tropical upper tropospheric trough (TUTT) across south Florida on July 16th shifted northwestward and closed off into an upper low over the northeastern Gulf on July 17th. The combination of deep tropical moisture and mid level cooler air overspread into northern Florida and Georgia supporting numerous showers and thunderstorms each afternoon and evening developing along the inland-moving sea breezes. A broad surface low then developed under the upper low in the northeastern Gulf and gradually deepened into Invest 91 on July 18th and then strengthened into Tropical Depression 2 on July 19th. Showers and thunderstorms rotated around the eastern side of the system shifting northward up the Florida peninsula July 19th into July 20th. A few strong to severe storms developed as the outer rainbands from TD 2 interacted with the sea breeze and outflow boundaries. On July 20th, mid-level drier air filtered into the area from the south triggering some stronger downbursts.
episodes.215958: A monsoonal pattern persisted onward through mid July, resulting in more instances of thunderstorm winds and flash flooding.
episodes.216340: A surface low pressure and cold front tracked through North Dakota, bringing scattered thunderstorms to the area. The only report of severe hail came from near Bremen in Wells County, and was one inch in diameter. Two tornadoes also occurred with these thunderstorms. One tornado started in Pierce County, northwest of Knox, and moved into Benson County. There was no known damage with this tornado so by NWS policy it is rated EF-U (Unknown). Another brief tornado developed southeast of Bremen in Wells County. There was no known damage with this tornado as well, so by NWS policy it is also rated EF-U (Unknown).
episodes.216357: A weak upper low was located over far southeast New Mexico while a surface trough was located along the Rio Grande Valley. Low level easterly flow brought good moisture into the El Paso area. A storm slowly moved south through northeast El Paso and with nearly an inch of rain in under an hour, flash flooding occurred.
episodes.216397: Widespread afternoon showers and thunderstorms erupted across southern Appalachian region on the 17th, affecting most of East Tennessee and far western North Carolina. These slow moving storms produced some isolated flooding reports in Cherokee county North Carolina.
episodes.216398: Widespread afternoon showers and thunderstorms erupted across southern Appalachian region on the 17th, affecting most of East Tennessee and far western North Carolina. These slow moving storms produced some isolated flooding reports in Knox county in Tennessee.
episodes.216505: Heavy rainfall caused irrigation canals along the Norwood River to overtop their banks. The flood remained over agricultural land and no major damage was reported.
episodes.216523: The region was along the edge of an area of high pressure from the 16th-18th. This positioning kept feeding in monsoonal moisture and instability to produce daily severe isolated severe thunderstorms to the region.
episodes.216584: Broad cyclonic flow aloft over the eastern Gulf and Florida peninsula coupled with a developing surface trough that would become the precursor to Tropical Storm Bertha created a favorable convective environment that produced a morning and afternoon round of storms that produced gusty marine winds across the Tampa Bay area waters northward to across the Nature Coast waters.
episodes.216585: Broad cyclonic flow aloft over the eastern Gulf and Florida peninsula coupled with a developing surface trough that would become the precursor to Tropical Storm Bertha created a favorable convective environment that produced severe hail near Brooksville in Hernando County.
episodes.216845: A man was struck by lightning on NE 12th St in Okeechobee and was airlifted to the hospital.
episodes.216846: Thunderstorms produced a waterspout, which become a tornado, and strong wind gusts along the Treasure Coast.
episodes.216847: A waterspout over the Indian River moved onshore in Indian River County.
episodes.216893: A slow moving storm system and abundant tropical moisture resulted in flash flooding across mainly the Northwest Hill Country and Northern Edwards Plateau.
episodes.216990: Monsoon moisture brought thunderstorms with heavy rain to San Bernardino County, resulting in flash flooding.
episodes.217053: Severe thunderstorms tracked north to south through the Devils Lake Basin during the evening hours producing damaging winds and several weak tornadoes. One tornado was EF-0 southwest of Maddock, ND in Benson County. The other did not have a damage indicator that could be rated as it passed into far northwest Benson County from Pierce County.
episodes.217060: Monsoon moisture brought thunderstorms with heavy rain and strong winds to much of Mohave County.
episodes.217102: Another multiple day period of unsettled weather occurred between July 17th and 19th across the Ohio Valley. On July 17th, the synoptic pattern featured weak flow through much of the troposphere, with the region being on the eastern side of an expansive upper ridge. However, hot and humid conditions were present, allowing for between 2000 and 3000 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE to develop across central Kentucky during the afternoon hours. Given the weak flow aloft, pulse convection was mainly experienced across the area, although a few stronger storm cores were able to produce downbursts resulting in isolated wind damage. Later in the evening, a cluster of storms across south central Kentucky congealed into a large mass of heavy rainfall, with precipitable water values exceeding 2 inches and decreasing instability allowing for efficient rainfall production. This resulted in isolated instances of flash flooding near Green River Lake. On the 18th, an approaching cold front and mid-level trough helped to increase the wind shear and forcing for storms, with more organized convection developing during the afternoon and evening hours. The strongest storm of the day went across the southwest side of the Louisville metro, producing several instances of wind damage. Finally, as the cold front sank to the south during the afternoon on July 19th, training thunderstorms in a rich moisture environment once again produced isolated flash flooding, this time in Cumberland and Clinton County.
episodes.217151: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the North Carolina mountains during the late afternoon. One of the storms produced a small area of damaging wind gusts in Madison County.
episodes.217165: A slow moving front meandered over the region July 15 and 16 resulting in scattered storms that produced damaging winds, particularly over southeastern PA and South Jersey.
episodes.217266: A few storms impacted south-central MT, producing gusts up to 73 mph and hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter.
episodes.217279: Weakening high pressure aloft allowed diurnal showers and thunderstorms to develop. Some storms near boundary interactions were able to become strong to severe.
episodes.217296: Continuing an active monsoon period with heavy rainfall caused running washes and rivers that led to impassable roadways.  Additionally, there was 2 deaths in the Santa Cuz river due to drowning.
episodes.217299: Active monsoon period continues with flash flooding across the Tucson Metro that led to multiple road closures and a death in the Julian Wash due to flooding.

The track is based on Sentinel satellite analysis showing scarring associated with the tornado tracking to the southeast towards where the damage to the trees and barns were filmed. Width is approximated from scarring visible on Sentinel satellite with the maximum width occurring to the southwest of Legreid Lake early on in the lifecycle. Maximum wind speed estimated at 85 mph.

A twelve-mile stretch of SR-88, between Mileposts 228-240, closed due to flooding damage sustained from 2-3 inches rain that fell the night of the 16th and the morning of the 17th. Flood damage included rockfalls, clogged culverts and drains, and portions of the road that were washed away. This stretch of the road was closed for approximately one week for repairs. Timing of impacts on the 16th estimated from radar. No injuries reported.

The Batesville area was impacted by flooding along the Leona River triggered by heavy rain concentrated in Uvalde County north of Batesville. Initial rises on the Leona River on July 16 flooded portions of US57 near Batesville. A much more significant rise occurred in the early morning of July 17, when floodwaters along the Leona River reached the community between 0000 and 0200CST, causing widespread flooding.||Inundation spread across much of the eastern half of Batesville and extended to FM117, impacting many residences east and some west of the highway. The greatest inundation extent was observed in southeastern portions of Batesville, where floodwaters reached a �� mile away from the Leona River. Flooding was observed along Main Street, Old Loma Vista Road, and adjacent roads. Around 70 families reported flood damage to their homes and belongings, with water levels reaching as high as 3ft inside. Approximately 120 people relocated to shelters. While floodwaters reached Batesville School, the campus sustained minimal damage. Batesville was isolated due to the flooding and subsequent closures of US57, FM117, and other surrounding roads.
Cibecue Creek stream gauge (CBQA3) measured a 4.27 foot rise, with a peak flow of 2294 cfs.
A USGS gauge along Sycamore Creek just west of SR-87 measured a rapid 3 foot rise and making Forest Service Road 402, a low-water crossing, impassable. No damages or injuries reported.

A major flood wave on the Nueces River triggered by torrential rain primarily over Uvalde County moved into Dimmit County on July 17 and caused extensive inundation of the floodplain in Dimmit County. Satellite imagery indicated the width of inundation spanned up to 2 miles in width over the lower Nueces River and along Soldier Slough. The Nueces River at Asherton remained at Major flood stage between July 17 and July 24, recording a crest of 31.56ft on July 18.||Damage to public infrastructure in Dimmit County amounted to around $1.4 million with damage primarily wrought to roadway infrastructure, water control facilities, and other utilities. Twenty-eight homes in the county were damaged or destroyed. The greatest amount of inundation in residential areas occurred in the Espantosa Subdivision and areas around Midway Park, where mandatory evacuations were ordered. Several roads in Dimmit County were closed due to flooding including FM65, FM189, FM1019, FM1433, and Highway 85. Flood damage to water wells resulted in a water shortage in Carrizo Springs with water service disruptions continuing into mid-August.
Tonto Creek stream gauge (TNRA3) measured a 4.22 foot rise.  Times are estimated.
